raw_text:
Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is an idiopathic cardiomyopathy presenting with heart failure secondary to left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction toward the end of pregnancy or in the months after delivery, when no alternative cause is identified. The historical “last month of pregnancy to 5 months postpartum” definition remains useful for research continuity, but contemporary definitions emphasize clinical exclusion of other causes and LV ejection fraction (LVEF) usually <45%, with or without LV dilatation [1-5]. PPCM is therefore best viewed not as a single uniform disease, but as a pregnancy-triggered syndrome in susceptible myocardium.

Epidemiology varies strikingly by geography, ancestry, ascertainment, and case definition. In the United States, population-based studies suggest rising incidence and disproportionate disease burden among Black women, older mothers, and those with hypertensive disorders or multiple gestation [6-8]. A Scottish 20-year population study confirmed substantial morbidity, including death, mechanical circulatory support, or transplantation in a minority, and showed that recovery is incomplete in many women [9]. Global registry data underscore heterogeneity: PPCM occurs across continents, but 6-month and 1-year mortality, thromboembolism, rehospitalization, medication use, and LV recovery differ by region [10-12]. In the North American IPAC cohort, most women improved substantially within 12 months, but baseline LVEF, LV size, and race were important predictors of recovery [13].

Pathogenesis is multifactorial. Genetic studies have reshaped the field by demonstrating overlap between PPCM and dilated cardiomyopathy. Truncating variants, especially in TTN, are enriched in PPCM cohorts, and broader sequencing has implicated additional cardiomyopathy genes such as FLNC, DSP, and BAG3 [14,15]. These findings support a “two-hit” model in which pregnancy-associated haemodynamic, vascular, hormonal, and inflammatory stress unmasks latent myocardial susceptibility. Genetic counselling and cardiomyopathy gene testing should be considered, particularly with severe disease, family history, arrhythmia, or incomplete recovery [16].

Mechanistic work has highlighted vascular and hormonal injury. In a landmark experimental model, oxidative stress promoted cathepsin-D cleavage of prolactin into an antiangiogenic 16-kDa fragment, producing endothelial and myocardial injury; bromocriptine prevented disease in mice [17]. Complementary models showed that angiogenic imbalance, including excess soluble fms-like tyrosine kinase-1 (sFlt1), can precipitate PPCM and may explain links with preeclampsia and multiple gestation [18]. MicroRNA-146a, induced by 16-kDa prolactin, may transfer endothelial injury signals to cardiomyocytes and has been proposed as both biomarker and therapeutic target [19]. In IPAC, higher sFlt1 and lower relaxin-2 were associated with PPCM biology and outcomes, supporting translational relevance of angiogenic pathways [20]. Contemporary reviews integrate these data into a vascular–hormonal hypothesis while emphasizing that no single pathway explains all cases [21]. Recent IPAC biomarker work further supports cathepsin-D as a marker linked to adverse outcome phenotypes [30].

Diagnosis requires vigilance because dyspnoea, fatigue, oedema, and tachycardia overlap with normal late pregnancy and puerperium. Red flags include orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, pulmonary oedema, hypoxaemia, new murmurs, syncope, arrhythmia, thromboembolism, or persistent symptoms after delivery. Initial evaluation should include electrocardiography, natriuretic peptide testing, troponin when clinically indicated, renal and liver function, thyroid studies when appropriate, and urgent echocardiography. Differential diagnoses include preeclampsia-related pulmonary oedema with preserved systolic function, pulmonary embolism, spontaneous coronary artery dissection, myocarditis, Takotsubo syndrome, valvular disease, congenital heart disease, sepsis, anaemia, thyroid disease, and toxic or familial cardiomyopathy.

Management is multidisciplinary and depends on pregnancy status, haemodynamic stability, fetal maturity, and breastfeeding goals. Antepartum therapy uses pregnancy-compatible heart failure treatment: loop diuretics for congestion, beta-blockers, hydralazine–nitrates for afterload reduction, and anticoagulation when LVEF is severely reduced or thrombus is present. Angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers, angiotensin receptor–neprilysin inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists, and sodium–glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors are avoided during pregnancy, but standard guideline-directed heart failure therapy should be initiated postpartum when compatible with lactation and maternal condition. Severe presentations require intensive care, early cardio-obstetric planning, vasopressors or inotropes selected cautiously, mechanical circulatory support when needed, and delivery only for obstetric indications or refractory maternal instability.

Bromocriptine, by suppressing prolactin, is the leading disease-specific therapy. A South African proof-of-concept trial and a German randomized multicentre study suggested improved LV recovery in selected severe PPCM, but trials were small and differed in design [22,23]. Meta-analysis suggests possible improvement in survival and LVEF, but evidence remains insufficient for universal use; if prescribed, bromocriptine should be accompanied by anticoagulation because of thrombotic risk and individualized discussion about lactation suppression [24]. Current pregnancy guidelines recommend expert-centre management, pregnancy heart teams, tailored heart failure therapy, and structured counselling [25].

Prognosis ranges from full recovery to chronic heart failure, arrhythmia, thromboembolism, transplant, or death. Recovery commonly occurs in the first 6–12 months, but late improvement and late deterioration both occur. Subsequent pregnancy is a major counselling issue: relapse risk is highest with persistent LV dysfunction, but recurrence can occur despite normalized LVEF [26]. Systematic reviews confirm wide variation in recovery, mortality, and recurrence, reflecting geography, severity, treatment access, and study design [27-29]. Long-term follow-up is therefore essential, including serial imaging, medication optimization, contraception counselling, cardiovascular risk reduction, and family screening when genetic disease is suspected.
